File_Name: Global satellite survey reveals uncertainty in landfill methane emissions.pdf (and p3.pdf)
Title: Global satellite survey reveals uncertainty in landfill methane emissions
Authors: C. Maasakkers et al. / GHGSat Research Consortium
Research_Objective: Quantify point-source methane emissions across 151 global waste sites using high-resolution satellite imagery and benchmark against reported inventories.
Study_Location: Global (151 waste sites across 6 continents)
Methodology_AI_Models: High-resolution satellite plume detection (GHGSat ~25m), Integrated Methane Enhancement (IME) mass-balance inversion, comparative inventory analysis.
Datasets_Used: 1,447 GHGSat observations across 151 landfills; national reported inventories (EPA GHGRP, UNFCCC, WasteMAP).
Main_Findings_NumericalResults: Substantial disagreement between observed satellite emissions and facility inventories (R2 near zero); managed sanitary landfills emitted ~50% less methane per area than open dumps.
AuthorStatedLimitations: High detection threshold (~100-200 kg/h); clear-sky overpass bias; intermittent snapshot sampling fails to capture temporal emission dynamics.
OurAssessmentLimitations: Does not detect fires or surface temperatures; cannot be used alone for continuous hazard early-warning without persistent ground sensing.
Relevance_MethaneHotspot: Very High (Establishes satellite plume detection capability at facility scale)
Relevance_FireThermalRisk: Low (No fire, thermal, or combustion indicators)
Relevance_MultiSourceFusion: High (Directly highlights the urgent need to fuse satellite observations with ground operational data)
PotentialContribution: Provides baseline satellite plume dataset (GHGSat_detected_plumes.csv) and empirical proof of model-measurement uncertainty.

Main_Findings_NumericalResults: Identified cumulative 230 ± 15 t/h of methane emissions from 38 landfills; hyperspectral sensors demonstrated cross-instrument consistency within 15–20%.
AuthorStatedLimitations: Cloud cover limits revisit frequency; sensitivity threshold ~500–1000 kg/h; strong-emitter selection bias.
OurAssessmentLimitations: Focuses strictly on massive super-emitters; does not detect moderate leaks, subsurface fires, or ground temperatures.
Relevance_MethaneHotspot: Very High (Direct source for data/data/landfills_hyper_obs.xlsx and NetCDF cases)

File_Name: Thermal hotspot detection in landfills using high-resolution land surface temperature data_ A case study of active and closed sites.pdf
Title: Thermal hotspot detection in landfills using high-resolution land surface temperature data: A case study of active and closed sites
Authors: S. E. et al. (Istanbul Technical University)
Research_Objective: Downscale Landsat 8/9 Land Surface Temperature (LST) from 100m to 10m using Sentinel-2 spectral indices and detect persistent thermal hotspots in landfills.
Study_Location: Istanbul, Turkey (Odayeri active sanitary landfill and Kemerburgaz closed dumpsite)
Methodology_AI_Models: Automated Machine Learning (AutoML), Neural Networks, Gaussian Process Regression, NDVI/NDBI/NDWI spatial downscaling, Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis.
Datasets_Used: Landsat 8/9 Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS) LST + Sentinel-2 MSI multispectral imagery (2023–2024).
Main_Findings_NumericalResults: Downscaled LST achieved RMSE of 0.74–2.38 °C; identified persistent subsurface thermal zones (>40 °C) in both active filling areas and closed unmanaged sections.
AuthorStatedLimitations: Surface LST is an indirect proxy for subsurface heat; thermal anomalies require ground verification; no direct gas concentration coupling.
OurAssessmentLimitations: High surface temperature can stem from solar heating of bare soil/dark plastic liners rather than biological exothermic reaction or fire; validation requires gas data.
Relevance_MethaneHotspot: Medium (Thermal anomalies often correlate with decomposition hotspots)
Relevance_FireThermalRisk: Very High (Directly demonstrates satellite thermal hotspot detection methodology)
Relevance_MultiSourceFusion: Very High (Fuses Landsat thermal band with Sentinel-2 optical bands)

File_Name: k6.pdf (Development of a subsurface landfill fire risk-index)
Title: Development of a conceptual framework for risk assessment of elevated internal temperatures in landfills
Authors: M. A. et al. (Waste Management / MDNR Bridgeton Study)
Research_Objective: Develop an empirical Risk of Subsurface Elevated Temperatures (RSET) index for early detection of subsurface smouldering fires using gas well data.
Study_Location: Bridgeton Landfill, Missouri, United States
Methodology_AI_Models: Multi-parameter gas ratio evaluation, Decision Trees, Statistical association testing, RSET threshold scoring (Low/Medium/High risk).
Datasets_Used: 18,469 gas wellhead observations (2013–2018) tracking CH4, CO2, O2, N2, temperature, and CH4/CO2 ratio.

AuthorStatedLimitations: Developed on a single massive landfill incident; threshold transferability to other sites requires local recalibration.
OurAssessmentLimitations: Requires internal gas well sampling; cannot be measured directly by high-altitude satellites.
Relevance_MethaneHotspot: High (Explains why methane drops when subsurface combustion consumes hydrocarbons)
Relevance_FireThermalRisk: Extremely High (Foundational ground-truth paper on chemical signatures of landfill fires)
Relevance_MultiSourceFusion: High (Combines multi-gas concentrations, gas ratios, and internal temperatures)
PotentialContribution: Provides the explicit classification labels and scientific rules for dataset k6_bridgeton_full_monitoring_dataset_18469_rows.xlsx.
